extracted.intended_audience: music theorists, musicology graduate students, and analysts of programmatic/narrative music
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Roland Barthes's S/Z system (the narrative codes) as a structured technique for close analysis of programmatic/orchestral music (here: Janácek's The Fiddler's Child), combining musical, affective, and programmatic information in segmented readings and diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proairetic code
rubrics_metrics.description: The proairetic code: The musical structure as determined by the succession of keys, motives, tempo, voice leading, and prolongation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proairetic material as the code of action/sequence (the 'chassis' into which other codes are set). In practice this is investigated via formal/key/tempo/motivic/voice-leading analysis (Table 1). Because it is defined by a particular sequence, represent the proairetic code in a diagram showing the entire code at once rather than interrupting it into small segmented lexias (author excludes it from segmented listings and places it in Example 3). Use linear presentations of key centers and sections to show overall form and progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semic code (motivic analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semic: The tracing of motives, their appearances, transpositions, and transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on motives as the semic code: list principal motives, their altered forms, first-appearance measure numbers, cellular structure, and any programmatic designations (Example 1). Classify motives as cyclic (pervade whole work, signify principal themes/characters/emotions) or situation motives (limited to sections/scenes and cease when situation changes). Indicate musical elements (realm 1) in parentheses (e.g., (MOT), (KEY), (TEX)). Track variations such as sequence, alteration, augmentation, diminution, and link motivic variation to dramatic function (e.g., motive d representing the mayor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermeneutic code
rubrics_metrics.description: Hermeneutic: The presentation, suspending, and solving of enigmas which occur in the music. They may be tonal, melodic, textural, harmonic, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify enigmas posed and their prolongation (small vs. major enigmas). Tag occurrences of a single enigma across the piece and gather them together to show statement, development, and resolution (the author collects all occurrences of Enigma #1 as an example). Use braces {HER} in segment annotations. Note that hermeneutic comprehensibility can suffer if treated alone; study interdependence with other codes/realms. Enigmas can be chromatic/pitch-based (e.g., recurring F♭) or texturally signaled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referential code
rubrics_metrics.description: Referential: Refers to other music by the same composer or by other composers, and other types of music or sounds. It may also refer to phenomena or knowledge outside of music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the referential code to make extrafluent comparisons (to other works, genres, literature, history, art, or non-musical phenomena). Mark references with braces {REF} or discuss them in [REF] commentary. The author reintroduces this code to allow comparisons across Janácek's works and other composers (e.g., offstage chorus analogies, or similarity to folk practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic code (noted and judged least relevant to music)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic: The symbolic antitheses prevalent in classical literature (e.g., life/death, hot/cold, youth/age).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barthes formulated a symbolic code, but the author follows McCreless in treating the symbolic code as a vestige of the referential code and 'the least relevant to music'—therefore it may be omitted in musical applications. If used, treat symbolic oppositions cautiously and consider overlap with referential/affective meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realm 1 — Absolute music
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute music involves musical elements and their relationships considered without recourse to either affect or program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realm 1 includes the proairetic code and the semic code and covers motives, key, harmony, pitch, texture/orchestration, dynamics, rhythm, and tempo. Indicate these elements in segment annotations using parentheses (e.g., (MOT), (KEY), (HAR), (TEX), (DYN), (RHY), (TEM)). Treat these as 'fundamental properties' and record their measurable musical features before connecting them to affect or program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realm 2 — Affective (emotive) realm
rubrics_metrics.description: Affective: The psychological impression of the musical elements (emotive connotations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark affective impressions with vertical lines (I AFF I) in segment annotations. Use theory of musical emotion (Meyer, Ferguson, Kivy, Cooke) to justify affective readings but note individual interpretation variance. Consider how affect prompts listener association of music with plot/character, and how affective readings interact with motivic identification (e.g., a motive may signal character via affective connotation or independently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Realm 3 — Programmatic realm
rubrics_metrics.description: Program: The association of musical elements and their psychological impression with textual information (poems, narratives, composer commentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use program sources (e.g., the poem [POEM], composer essay [JAN]) and encode programmatic associations in square brackets [POEM], [JAN], [PRO]. Mark programmatic impressions of musical elements as [PRO]. Treat programmatic information as an input to be combined with musical and affective data rather than as an overriding explanation; use it to justify motive-character links, extra-musical referents, and narrative events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segmentation into lexias/segments (Barthes method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section the musical text into segments (lexia) and for each segment identify which of the codes are operative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt Barthes's approach of breaking the work into numbered segments (Barthes used 561 lexias in S/Z). Present each segment, then indicate which codes operate there (e.g., (MOT)... I AFF I ... [POEM] ... {HER}). Use cross-references among segments to track reappearances and code interplay. The author returns to Barthes's style of organization (listing segments and the codes operating for each). Note: exclude proairetic from segmented listings and treat it diagrammatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notational encoding conventions for multi-realm annotations
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of punctuation and abbreviations to differentiate types of information and codes in segment annotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use four punctuation conventions: parentheses for musical elements (Realm 1), vertical lines for affective connotations (Realm 2), square brackets for programmatic materials (Realm 3), and braces for hermeneutic and referential codes. Employ abbreviations given in Table 3: (MOT), (KEY), (HAR), (PIT), (TEX), (DYN), (RHY), (TEM); I AFF I; [POEM], [JAN], [PRO]; {HER}, {REF}. This legible encoding helps readers differentiate simultaneous parameters in a dense annotated listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent the proairetic/formal structure diagrammatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the proairetic code resists interruption, show the proairetic code (key/tempo/motive succession) in a diagram representing the entire sequence/large-scale form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce a linear presentation of key centers and sections (as in Example 3) and divide the piece into large parts and subsections. Use boxed ritornelli and annotated measures to show key relationships and recurring tonal areas. This complements the segmented lexia listing and clarifies long-range structural relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace flow and interaction between realms and codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how information flows among the three realms (absolute, affective, programmatic) and between them and Barthes's codes (Table 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map interactions in each segment: e.g., how a motivic (Realm 1) feature triggers an affective reading (Realm 2) which in turn supports a programmatic inference (Realm 3), or how referential links feed back into hermeneutic resolution. Use diagrams or tabular flow charts if helpful. Recognize that multiple routes (motivic->affect->program; referential->absolute->hermeneutic, etc.) are possible and important for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify motives as cyclic vs situation motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate motives that pervade the whole work (cyclic) from those limited to particular areas (situation motives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note which motives recur throughout (signifying principal themes/characters/emotions) and which are confined to scenes or situations and then disappear. Record first-appearance measures, derived forms, and functional behavior (e.g., motive d as the mayor; motives e–i as situation motives). Use motivic distribution to support programmatic/character identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and present occurrences of single enigmas
rubrics_metrics.description: For hermeneutic clarity, gather all occurrences of a single enigma (e.g., a pitch or motive that repeatedly puzzles) into one place to show its development and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After segment-by-segment annotation, summarize the trajectory of a given enigma by quoting/collecting its instances and related affective/programmatic inferences (the author compiles all instances of Enigma #1—F♭—as an example). This aids readability and demonstrates how suspense is maintained or resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use programmatic primary sources as explicit inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: In programmatic analysis, use the originating textual sources (poem/story) and composer commentary as primary programmatic data to link musical elements to narrative/content meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite poem text passages ([POEM]) and composer essay remarks ([JAN]) when assigning programmatic referents to motives/sections. Cross-check musical evidence (motivic recurrence, affect) with explicit program statements from the author/composer. Treat these program sources as part of Realm 3 rather than automatically privileging them over musical readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow reading—plural, multi-parameter analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Barthes's principal aim: to slow down the reading of a work so the plurality of meaning from multiple codes and realms is exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dense, local-detail annotation over a brisk linear reading. The technique's advantage is revealing the interplay among musical elements, affect, program, and codes; linear analysis cannot handle more than a few parameters simultaneously. Avoid exclusive reliance on one code or realm; combine them to reveal textual plurality and interpretive richness.
